answer.label: Not Dr. Seuss — actually Robert Fulghum
answer.sourceLine: The thought and the original wording come from Robert Fulghum’s 1997 book True Love, not from Dr. Seuss. Fulghum actually wrote “…fall into mutually satisfying weirdness—and call it love—true love”; the popular “fall in mutual weirdness” line is a trimmed-down paraphrase that later got pinned on Seuss. Per Quote Investigator, Geisel died in 1991—six years before the book appeared.

source.excerpt: We’re all a little weird. And life is a little weird. And when we find someone whose weirdness is compatible with ours, we join up with them and fall into mutually satisfying weirdness—and call it love—true love.
trail: 1997: Robert Fulghum publishes the line in True Love, in a section titled “Perspective,” per Quote Investigator.
2007: A trimmed version—“mutual weirdness,” no “true love”—runs in the Journal-Standard of Freeport, Illinois credited to “Author Unknown,” as QI documents.
~2011: The altered wording gets reassigned to Dr. Seuss—chronologically impossible, since Wikiquote also credits the line to Fulghum’s True Love.
Today: It circulates on cards, mugs, and social media as “Dr. Seuss”—a textbook feel-good misattribution.
source.excerptNote: Fulghum’s original wording. The viral “fall in mutual weirdness and call it love” version drops “mutually satisfying” and the closing “true love.”

source.rightsNote: The line was first published in Robert Fulghum’s True Love in 1997, so in the United States it remains under copyright; rights rest with the author and his publisher. The Dr. Seuss attribution is not only wrong but chronologically impossible—Geisel died in 1991.

author.name: Robert Fulghum
author.heading: About Robert Fulghum
author.bio: Robert Fulghum is an American author and former Unitarian Universalist minister, best known for the mega-selling essay collection All I Really Need to Know I Learned in Kindergarten (1988). His warm, aphoristic style is exactly the kind of writing that gets stripped of attribution online—and, ironically, reassigned to other famous names. The weirdness-and-love passage comes from his 1997 book True Love.

misattribution.heading: How Dr. Seuss got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a double distortion: the wrong author and the wrong words. The idea and the original phrasing are Robert Fulghum’s; the version that went viral is a trimmed paraphrase that drifted onto Dr. Seuss.

items.why: Geisel died in 1991, six years before Fulghum published the line in 1997. Quote Investigator calls the Seuss credit “too late chronologically and apparently spurious.”
Fulghum wrote “fall into mutually satisfying weirdness—and call it love—true love.” A 2007 newspaper reprint shortened it to “mutual weirdness” and dropped “true love,” per QI.

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is Robert Fulghum, from his 1997 book True Love—and even the popular wording is a later, trimmed-down version of what he actually wrote (source).

context.heading: Why it spread
lead: The line is warm, quotable, and reassuring—precisely the profile of a quote that loses its author on the way around the internet. Once the trimmed 2007 newspaper version was floating free as “Author Unknown,” it needed only a famous, cuddly name to attach to, and Dr. Seuss—already the internet’s go-to for feel-good aphorisms—was the natural magnet.
The irony is that Robert Fulghum, its actual author, is himself a household name for gentle wisdom. He simply lost a coin-flip with a more marketable one.
context.pull: The wrong author and the wrong words — a double distortion.
